Six Demands, One Closed Strait

Iran has turned the Strait of Hormuz into a geopolitical toll booth — and handed Washington the bill.

The Revolutionary Guards say the strait will reopen only if the United States accepts Iran’s terms in full. Tehran insists this has nothing to do with its talks with Oman, even as both countries negotiate new shipping arrangements. 

In Middle Eastern diplomacy, two tracks are “unrelated” until they become the same deal.

Iran’s Supreme National Security Council has reportedly named its price: end threats against Iran, stop the war against Iran and its allies, withdraw U.S. forces from the region, pay compensation, lift every sanction and release frozen Iranian assets without conditions.

The offer is simple enough for a corporate slide deck: Washington makes sweeping concessions; Tehran reopens the world’s energy artery. Iran does not call this coercion. It calls it a new regional order.

For Tehran, Hormuz is not merely a commercial route. It is part of Iran’s “geographic and strategic power.” 

The emerging Iran-Oman arrangement would reportedly steer inbound ships through waters near Iran and outbound traffic via Oman — making every tanker a daily acknowledgment of Iranian leverage.

Washington calls it extortion. Tehran calls it sovereignty. Shipping insurers will call it a reason to raise premiums.

A narrow stretch of water carries an enormous share of global oil and gas. When one regional power uses it as a bargaining chip, the costs do not stay in the Gulf. 

They arrive at gas stations, in electricity bills and at grocery stores.

📣 Brazil stablecoins face IMF scrutiny as crypto flows outpace capital 

🌐 IMF has called for closer oversight of Brazil’s stablecoin market as cross-border crypto flows outpace traditional capital movements. The report says cross-border crypto transactions have increased faster than conventional capital flows and now require closer regulatory attention because of their growing links with the country’s financial system. The assessment says stablecoin purchases respond much more strongly to global financial shocks than traditional portfolio investment or foreign direct investment. 

🔔 Based on the IMF’s analysis, purchases of dollar-backed stablecoins are two to three times more sensitive to external market events, raising concerns over how quickly international volatility could spread through crypto markets. Brazil has emerged as one of the world’s more active crypto markets, with stablecoins accounting for a significant share of digital asset activity. The IMF said the country’s crypto ecosystem has become increasingly connected with the traditional financial sector, making regulatory oversight more important as adoption continues to rise.

⚠️ The report acknowledges that Banco Central do Brasil (BCB) has already introduced measures to regulate crypto asset service providers. Even so, the IMF said several areas still need stronger rules, including customer asset protection, stablecoin issuance requirements, and compliance with anti-money laundering (AML) and counter-terrorist financing (CFT) standards.
